title: Raffle Stub Lookup
story: You run the raffle at a school fair. The stubs of sold tickets are filed in one list from lowest number to highest. Not every number was sold, so there are gaps.
The head teacher reads out a winning number. Before anyone walks up, you want to know whether it was sold and where its stub sits.
task: Write findTicket(tickets, drawn). tickets is sorted from smallest to largest and has no repeats. Return the index of drawn in tickets, or -1 if that number was never sold.
Use the sorted order: your solution should look at about log₂ n stubs, not all of them. An empty list returns -1.
constraints: tickets is strictly increasing (sorted, no repeats).

examples.explanation: The middle stub, index 3, holds 488: found in one look.
The middle stub, 488, is less than 500, so look right: 519, 760, 901. Their middle, 760, is too big, so look left of it: just 519. Not 500 either, and nothing is left. Three looks.

hints: In the first example, look only at the middle stub, 488. If the drawn number were 700, which half could you throw away unread?
Because the list is sorted, one look at the middle rules out half of what is left. Keep the still-possible part as a range from lo to hi.
Each round, look at the middle of the range. Equal: done. Too small: the answer is to the right, so move lo past the middle. Too big: move hi before it. When does the range become empty?
Start with lo = 0 and hi = n - 1. Loop while lo <= hi (the = matters: a one-stub range still needs checking). Set mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2) and compare. If the loop ends, return -1.
bruteForce: Read the stubs from the start until you find the number or run out. Correct and simple.
But with 100,000 stubs one call can take 100,000 looks, ignoring that the list is sorted. Binary search needs about 17, because 2¹⁷ is more than 100,000.

py: def find_ticket(tickets: list[int], drawn: int) -> int:

tests.note: last ticket: catches loops that stop one step early

js: if (tickets[mid] < drawn) lo = mid + 1; // answer is to the right
else hi = mid - 1;                      // answer is to the left
return -1; // the range is empty: never sold
py: lo = mid + 1  # answer is to the right
hi = mid - 1  # answer is to the left
return -1  # the range is empty: never sold
walkthrough: In a sorted list, one comparison rules out half the candidates. Keep a range [lo, hi] where the number could still be, and halve it each round.
• lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3. 488 < 500, so index 3 and below are too small. lo = 4.
• lo = 4, hi = 6, mid = 5. 760 > 500, so index 5 and above are too big. hi = 4.
• Now lo = 4 is past hi = 3. The range is empty, so return -1.
In step 3 the range held a single stub and still had to be checked. That is why the loop runs while lo <= hi, not lo < hi. With <, searching for 901 would never look at the last stub.
The moves are mid + 1 and mid - 1, never just mid: you already checked mid. Keeping it can stop the range shrinking and loop forever.
solution.timeWhy: Each round halves the range, so about log₂ n rounds.
solution.takeaway: In a sorted list, compare with the middle and throw away the half that cannot hold the answer. Keep an inclusive range lo..hi, loop while lo <= hi, and always move past mid. The other binary searches in this set change what you compare and which half you keep, but the halving is the same.
